story: Savraj S. Grewal was last author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas, with Shrivani Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas as first author. PubMed lists the author at the Cumming School of Medicine of the University of Calgary.

In fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae, nutrient/TOR signalling in the fat body holds down the mitochondrial protein TFAM after transcription. This TOR to TFAM link in the fat body helps set how fast the whole animal grows.

studies.title: Nutrient/TOR signaling controls adipose mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) to regulate organismal growth in Drosophila
studies.finding: In Drosophila larvae, nutrient/TOR signaling in the fat body (a key nutrient-sensing tissue) post-transcriptionally suppresses the mitochondrial transcription factor TFAM, and this TOR→TFAM axis in fat-body tissue controls whole-body developmental growth — a mechanistic link between nutrient sensing and interorgan growth control via mitochondrial bioenergetics.

The team put cancer-linked DDX3X mutations into the yeast version of the gene, DED1. The mutant yeast grew despite rapamycin and made more protein from mRNAs with simple 5' ends once TORC1 was blocked. This is yeast work, so it suggests a mechanism and does not show it in tumours.

story: In cultured cells, AMPK turned out to restrain ULK1 and autophagy during glucose starvation or mitochondrial energy stress, the opposite of the usual textbook picture. AMPK also protected the ULK1 machinery from being broken down by caspases, so cells could restart autophagy later. Park is the first of three authors, and PubMed lists the University of Minnesota.

current.role: First author of the 2005 knock-in mouse study showing that ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation sets cell size and glucose handling.
current.sub: Department of Biochemistry, The Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School, Jerusalem, Israel
story: Igor Ruvinsky was first author of a 2005 mouse study in the Atlas, with Oded Meyuhas as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School in Jerusalem. The team made knock-in mice in which all five phosphorylatable serines of ribosomal protein S6 were changed to alanine, so S6 could not be phosphorylated.

Contrary to the model of the time, the mutation did not change the translation of 5'TOP mRNAs. Cells from these mice made protein faster and divided faster, yet were smaller, and rapamycin did not shrink them further. Pancreatic beta cells were also small, and the adult mice had low insulin and impaired glucose tolerance.

highlights.RUV2005: First author: made S6 phosphorylation-deficient knock-in mice and showed the cells and beta cells were small, with impaired glucose tolerance.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Biochemistry, The Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School, Jerusalem, Israel

studies.title: Ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation is a determinant of cell size and glucose homeostasis
studies.finding:
The authors made knock-in mice in which all five phosphorylatable serines of ribosomal protein S6 were replaced by alanine, so rpS6 could not be phosphorylated. Contrary to the then widely accepted model, translational control of 5'TOP mRNAs was unaffected. Fibroblasts from these mice made protein faster and divided faster, yet were smaller than wild-type cells, and rapamycin did not shrink them further, which points to rpS6 phosphorylation as a downstream effector of mTOR in cell-size control. Adult mutant mice also had smaller pancreatic beta-cells, less pancreatic insulin, low blood insulin and impaired glucose tolerance.

The paper found that SH3BP4 binds the inactive Rag GTPase complex when amino acids are scarce and stops it from becoming active. This keeps mTORC1 away from the lysosome, lowers mTORC1 activity and cell growth, and favors autophagy. PubMed lists Kim at the Department of Biochemistry, University of Minnesota.

story: Delong Meng was first author of a 2023 Oncogene paper in the Atlas (MEN2023), from UCSF with colleagues at Revolution Medicines. RMC-6272 blocks mTORC1 more than 25 times more strongly than mTORC2. It killed ER-positive breast cancer cell lines, especially those with PIK3CA or PTEN mutations, and still worked in hormone-therapy-resistant and CDK4/6-inhibitor-resistant models. current.role: First author of a 2018 study showing that mTOR sets the speed and strength of circadian clocks.
current.sub: Department of Biological Sciences · University of Memphis, USA
story: Blocking mTOR made circadian clocks run slower and flatter, and activating it made them run faster and stronger. This was seen in cultured cells, in brain (SCN) and liver tissue taken from mice, and in mice with one copy of the mTOR gene, whose activity rhythm ran longer. Ramanathan is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the University of Memphis.

highlights.RAM2018: First of eight authors on the study of mTOR and circadian clock period and amplitude.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, University of Memphis, Memphis, Tennessee, United States of America.

studies.title: mTOR signaling regulates central and peripheral circadian clock function
studies.finding: mTOR sets how fast and how strongly the circadian clock ticks. Inhibiting mTOR lengthened the clock period and flattened its amplitude; activating it shortened the period and raised the amplitude, in cells, in ex vivo brain (SCN) and liver clocks, and in mTOR heterozygous mice, whose locomotor rhythm ran longer. The study starts from the observation that mTOR activity itself oscillates over 24 hours in many tissues.

story: Edward J. Brignole is a middle author on three structural papers in the Atlas, all with David M. Sabatini as senior author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Biology of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and at MIT.nano.

The 2018 paper gives cryo-EM structures of GATOR1, alone and bound to the Rag GTPases. The 2019 paper shows how Raptor docks onto Rag-Ragulator, so that mTORC1 can reach the lysosome. The 2022 paper gives the structure of human GATOR2, a large cage-like complex; the study notes that how GATOR2 inhibits GATOR1 is still not fully settled. All three are structures of purified proteins, not studies in animals or people.

studies.title: Structure of the nutrient-sensing hub GATOR2
studies.finding: Cryo-EM structure of human GATOR2: a 1.1 MDa, two-fold symmetric cage built on an octagonal scaffold decorated with eight pairs of WD40 beta-propellers, and a map of where Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 dock. It substantially advances the GATOR2 side of the sensor module, though how GATOR2 inhibits GATOR1 is still not fully settled.

studies.title: Structural basis for the docking of mTORC1 on the lysosomal surface
studies.finding:
3.2-angstrom cryo-EM structure of Raptor bound to Rag-Ragulator, showing how Raptor reads out the nutrient-dependent nucleotide state of the Rag GTPases: one part of Raptor senses RagA's nucleotide state, a separate 'claw' senses RagC's, and both have to be in the correct nutrient-signalling combination before Raptor is allowed to dock. Mutating the contact points blocks mTORC1 from reaching the lysosome and inhibits its signalling, which is the functional evidence behind the structural claim. Combined with a separate structure of mTORC1 bound to its activator Rheb, the paper builds a model of the complete, active mTORC1 sitting on the lysosome.

current.sub: Department of Biology · University of Fribourg, Switzerland
story: The study found that malonyl-CoA, an intermediate in making fatty acids, binds directly to the catalytic pocket of mTOR and competes with ATP, so it works as a natural mTORC1 inhibitor. When fatty acid synthase levels fall, malonyl-CoA rises and turns mTORC1 down, tying fat-making capacity to overall growth output. Nicastro is the first of fourteen authors, and PubMed lists the University of Fribourg.

highlights.NIC2023: First of fourteen authors on the paper identifying malonyl-CoA as an ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Fribourg, Fribourg, Switzerland.

studies.finding: Malonyl-CoA, an intermediate of fatty-acid biosynthesis, binds the mTOR catalytic pocket directly and acts as a conserved ATP-competitive inhibitor of mTORC1; when fatty acid synthase is downregulated, rising malonyl-CoA feeds back to dampen mTORC1 activity, linking lipogenic capacity to overall biosynthetic output.

current.role: First author of a 2026 fruit fly study showing that rapamycin can lengthen or shorten life depending on the diet.
current.sub: Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama, Mobile, Alabama
story: Lauren N. Jackson is first author of an Atlas study (JAC2026) in Drosophila fruit flies. Across five fly strains, rapamycin was harmful in 19 of 26 experiments on a cornmeal and torula yeast food. On a richer brewer's yeast food it helped in 8 experiments, did nothing in 14, and was never clearly harmful. Effects on median lifespan ranged from a 51 percent loss to a 5 percent gain, and depended on sex and strain. PubMed lists Jackson at the University of South Alabama.

highlights.JAC2026: First author: reported that rapamycin's effect on fly lifespan flips between harmful and helpful depending on diet, sex and strain.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Biomedical Sciences, HAHN 4025, University of South Alabama, 5721 USA Drive N, Mobile, AL, 36688-0002, USA.

studies.title: Diet-dependent, beneficial and adverse effects of rapamycin on life span of Drosophila melanogaster
studies.finding: Rapamycin's effect on Drosophila lifespan is highly diet-dependent: on a cornmeal/torula-yeast medium it was harmful in 19 of 26 experiments across 5 strains, but on a nutrient-rich brewer's-yeast medium it was beneficial in 8 and neutral in 14, with no significant harm. Effects on median lifespan ranged from -51.3% to +5.4%, varying by sex and strain; rapamycin was also toxic to development at 10-200 µM.

The team found that mTORC2 promotes de novo synthesis of fats and lipids, and that blocking fatty acid or sphingolipid synthesis prevented tumours. Higher lipid synthesis also tracked with mTORC2 activity in liver cancer patients.
Markus Heim is a middle author on the paper, and PubMed lists the affiliation shown here. Other Atlas records under this name show no affiliation in PubMed, so they are not included.

David Allison is a middle author, and PubMed lists him in the Department of Biostatistics at the University of Alabama, Birmingham. A second Atlas record under this name carries no affiliation, so it is not included.

current.role: Co-author (middle position in the author list) of the Atlas studies BAS2012, PIC2014.
current.sub: Department of Breast Medical Oncology, Cancer Institute Hospital, Japanese Foundation for Cancer Research, Tokyo, Japan
story: BAS2012 (2012) is BOLERO-2, a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. Adding everolimus to exemestane roughly doubled progression-free survival (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review). Yoshinori Ito is a middle author in the author list. PIC2014 (2014) is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2.
